utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that there are no preliminaries. Therefore, could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nikolic. Please be seated. Mr. Nikolic, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. We hope to conclude your testimony today. Mr. Petrusic will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, I have taken your suggestions into account so that today there will be no repetitive questions that have already been heard in this courtroom, and I hope that we will proceed much faster.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nikolic, we're still dealing with the 13th of July. What I would like to ask you is whether you received and from whom you received information that General Mladic would pass along that route from Konjevic Polje -- from Bratunac towards Konjevic Polje and on, on the 13th of July, and that in general he was going to leave the Bratunac area.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, I already said that the information that General Mladic was going to go along that route on that day came from the military police commander, Mirko Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: But you don't have reliable information from where Mirko Jankovic got this information?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. There was probably an order for a section of the Bratunac Brigade Military Police to be engaged, so the person who issued the order probably knows where that information came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, the beginning of your answer, "I don't know," is good enough. What probably may have been the case is not relevant. You don't know. Please proceed, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, could General Mladic have passed and gone towards Milici or towards Han Pijesak and Crna Rijeka, his final destination, along a different route without passing through Sandici and Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he could have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Was it possible to expect in view of the situation on the road and the general situation in the Bratunac and Konjevic Polje and Nova Kasaba area with a large number of armed Muslims who were transferring through that locality, so would it be reasonable to expect that General Mladic, his security, and his security organ, felt that it would have been safer to take a different route?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a hypothetical question. It's possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, there are five or six assumptions in your question which have not been verified first. And then whether it's possible, whether it's reasonable to expect asks for a judgement. So it's both hypothetical and there are four or five unexplained assumptions, and it is asking for opinion. That is not the type of questions that assist the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President. I will finish that particular topic. Can we look at document 65 ter 1D01002 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, while we're waiting for the document, do you know who Mladen Blagojevic is? Do you remember? A lot of time has passed since then, of course.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember very well, I think this is a policeman in the Bratunac Brigade Military Police Platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And do you know Milovan Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And was he also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: E-court on our left screens is not functioning well. We could, of course, meanwhile use our right screens but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that's no solution for the witness. Witness, can you see the document, which should be witness statement Mladen Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes I can see it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Our e-court is not working.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see it. Yes. And the statement is my language that I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that when we refer or read from the document that we do it very, very slowly and that everyone uses his other screen, which you can by choosing the right buttons --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters only have one screen and it's not working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was the reason why I asked that everything would be read very slowly because I was aware that it was not a solution for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, let me continue. You also know Milovan Mitrovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that we very slowly proceed and use as much as we can our right screens but with full understanding for the interpreters having no screen on which they can choose. Slowly, therefore, Mr. Petrusic, you may proceed. And meanwhile, within two or three minutes I do understand the system will function again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What about Slobodan Mijatovic, do you know him?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Borivoje Jakovljevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Pero Andric?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And would you agree that this paragraph, paragraph 5 in the B/C/S version, and paragraph 4 in the English version, names soldiers who belong to the Bratunac Brigade Military Police?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I already said that these were members of the Bratunac Brigade Military Police Platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the next paragraph of the statement, the witness states that on the 13th of July, seven or eight soldiers of the military police of the Bratunac Brigade --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now we don't have a transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We do, but is there ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I can follow the right monitor and turn the transcript on there but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The transcript in e-court is not functioning at the moment but in LiveNote it's going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Too many problems at this moment on too many screens. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We will take a short break of most likely no more than five minutes to -- to restart all systems. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: --- Break taken at 9.48 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness with escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Technical problems being resolved, Mr. Petrusic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, did you know that members of the military police, in the morning on the 13th of July, were driving General Mladic to the Suceska area to meet with units under the command of Milan Jolovic, Legenda?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you switch on the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You asked me if I knew that members of the military police were driving General Mladic. No, they were not driving him. They were in the escort of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And did you know that in the morning of the 13th of July, they were in the escort of General Mladic in the Suceska area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was saying -- I was saying, the witness has just told you the answer to the question you are just putting to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, would you agree with me that this part of the statement is correct, that after Sandici, in the escort, they came to Konjevic Polje? This is paragraph 3 in the Serbian version and paragraph 2 in the English version on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see the first page here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: It's the second page.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. And could you please tell me which paragraph it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the second -- in the Serbian version, it's paragraph 3, and in the English version, it's paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to reply to the previous question, to one part of the previous question because I did not give you an answer to that. So I don't agree with that and I did not have information that General Mladic, on the 13th, was in Suceska. I know and I have information, I have a report by the military police commander, that on the 13th, General Mladic was in Srebrenica at the municipal building or in the municipality of Srebrenica, that he toured the Orthodox church, and that he spoke with some people from the Srebrenica municipality, and then after that conversation he returned to Bratunac. So there is no reason, it's not logical, and it wouldn't be true that any forces were in the Suceska area at that time. The Wolves from the Drina were not in the Suceska sector on the 13th. If you take the map, you can see. I know that by heart. The Suceska sector has nothing to do with any of the axes of attack on Srebrenica. It's the birthplace of Zulfo Tursunovic, a man who was suspected, he was a commander of a notorious brigade which also committed crimes against the Serbian population, and that is that sector. So Suceska in any way would have been the objective of the visit by General Mladic. This is what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, after the completion of combat operations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry to intervene. No objection. I just think for the transcript, the last sentence of Mr. Nikolic's answer was -- in the transcript: "So Suceska in any way would have been the objective of the visit ..." It seems to me that there is something missing. "Would have been" or "would not have been."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Would not have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, we are now discussing paragraph 4 in the Serbian version and paragraph 3 in the English. Witness Blagojevic says here: "I am not sure whether General Mladic got out of his jeep, but I remember him shouting through the window or the open door at these policemen, who were obviously rather relaxed, and he criticised them for not doing anything, just sunbathing at all these check-points and stealing while the soldiers were dying for them. At this intersection, there were no persons for whom I could have concluded that they were captured Muslims." Now, when this witness speaks about the interjunction, he's referring to an interjunction in Konjevic Polje? What is your comment on this?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time that I am looking at this statement. I don't think it will be appropriate for me to comment upon it. I would have preferred if you had given me time to read it first and then ask me to give comments about the whole statement and the veracity and the strength of arguments of this statement. Just like on page 1, this portion is absolutely untrue. There is absolutely no connection because I know exactly what was going on in that period. I know exactly which route General Mladic took on the morning of the 13th until I saw him off from Konjevic Polje. So I know exactly where he was, with whom he was, where he had lunch, where he stopped. He stopped at Sandici. He got out of his vehicle. It is true that he argued with the police, because that was an ongoing conflict, and he criticised them for not doing their job properly. That was a verbal altercation. There were insults traded, et cetera. So that was a conflict between the police and the army stemming from the relationship between General Mladic and President Karadzic because their relationship was not good.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just tell you this: I know exactly what occurred. The stop was in Konjevic Polje and everything that I had explained before took place. And of course there was another stop in Nova Kasaba. This is a report I received from Mirko Jankovic and he in turn received a report from the policeman who escorted General Mladic to Han Pijesak. If you want to know what was really going on on that day, I still stand by to what I said and I claim that that is correct and nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, it's totally unclear what you would like to have comment on. You read the whole of a paragraph. Do you want to know whether this witness has any recollection of Mr. Mladic criticising the policemen, whether it's the right location he's talking about, whether these were civilian policemen or not civilian policemen? It's totally unclear what you seek to elicit from this witness. Asking for comment without any direction doesn't bring us any further. So please put focused questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, we're now going to move to paragraph 5 in the Serbian version and paragraph 4 in English, and I'm going to quote it. "I also state that on the occasion at the mentioned intersection on the 13th of July, I can say with certainly that I did not see Momir Nikolic speaking to General Mladic."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I object to the form of the question, Your Honour. My understanding of the practice of this Tribunal, and I believe in this courtroom as well, although I haven't practiced in here, is that this type of allegation -- I know exactly where my friend is going. He's now going to put it to Mr. Nikolic that he was lying, that this statement -- that question needs to be put to the witness not by reading out a witness statement, but first to put it to the witness and then, if necessary, he can refer to the statement. That's just what I'm used to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, it's common practice in this Court. I've emphasized quite a few things again and again, that before you put to a witness what another witness said on a subject on which the witness testifies, that you should first explore that and only then put that to the witness that another witness said something different. Could you please keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my point of departure was the fact that the witness already gave a statement about the encounter with Mr. Mladic in Konjevic Polje and that he explained the way in which this encounter occurred. All I'm trying now is to put to him a statement given by another witness, nothing more than that. And in line with that statement, I would like to hear his comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One of our problems, Mr. Petrusic, is that we do not know exactly whether what the witness in the document says is exactly about the same location, about the same event, et cetera, so therefore you should explore that in some detail. And a suggestion by the witness that he could read that statement perhaps during the next break and then tell -- tell us what -- where he thinks it's consistent or inconsistent with what he said and then briefly deal with that, might be a suggestion that should be adopted. But just to put bluntly before another statement and then to say well -- to suggest it's all the same, it's contradicting, et cetera, you should explore that in a systematic and organised way. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since I have a transcript as well -- but, okay, let's try it another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, you said that you are acquainted with Borivoje Jakovljevic, that he was an MP, that he was part of General Mladic's escort detail on the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Half of your statement is true. Half is not. I said that I knew Borivoje, that he was a member of the military police, but I did not say that he was in Mladic's escort because I did not know by name the persons that the military police commander assigned to escort him. I wasn't interested in that then and I'm still not interested to know who specifically was there, to know their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 65 ter document 1D1022. Page 28 through 32 in e-court. This is the Blagojevic case, 26th of May, 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, this witness who appeared in the Blagojevic case said that he hadn't seen you in Konjevic Polje, and that he was escorting General Mladic and that they stopped at Konjevic Polje but that he did not see you there. Do you refute the evidence given by this witness in the Blagojevic case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, what is the question? Is the question, could this witness tell us whether Mr. Jakovljevic saw him? He can tell whether he saw Mr. Jakovljevic. He says, "I don't know whether he was in the escort." He has been quite clear on that. How could you possibly know whether someone had seen you or not seen you. What's the -- could you explain to us how it is possible that this witness could tell us? And then if Mr. Jakovljevic didn't see Mr. Nikolic, there are various explanations. I think the witness could not help us with very much. Either he didn't look well, he was looking at a different direction, he did not recognise Mr. Nikolic. Whatever. What's the -- please think about your questions and about the evidence you seek to elicit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On that occasion when you had an encounter with General Mladic in Konjevic Polje, did you recognise any of the soldiers who were in the escorting vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really didn't pay attention to General Mladic's security detail because there were quite a few of them. My focus was on reporting to General Mladic and I did it in a proper military manner. I approached him and I reported to him. I wasn't looking around trying to identify either members of the police or other people who were around him, and there were many of them. And I cannot say with certainty, although I know them all, that I specifically identified and noticed any of them. In other words, I did not pay attention to them. I paid attention to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did they ever get out of the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A large group, some dozen of them constituted his escort when he arrived at Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did they get out of the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And amongst them, you were unable to recognise your own military policemen?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already gave you an answer to that question. My attention was focused on reporting. I wasn't looking around. You know how it's being done. I'm not looking around. I am just looking at the General and I am concentrated on reporting to him, and it never occurred to me to look around in order to identify the persons escorting General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 1D01006 from 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, as you can see, this is a statement given by Mile Petrovic that you spoke about in the past few days. He was together with Mirko Jankovic in an APC. On page 3 in Serbian, line 7 from the bottom in the second paragraph, and line 8 from the bottom of the page in the first paragraph also in English. You can see that when Mile Petrovic was giving this statement at the police station in Bratunac on the 25th of August, 2003, and while he was describing this particular event, I'm going to paraphrase what he said, that he had gone and killed a number of Muslim men in order to revenge his brother. And in that respect he says the following: "I can say that I read in the newspaper and heard from other citizens that they also read in the papers that Momir Nikolic accused me in his statement that during the ride in the armoured personnel carrier from Bratunac to Konjevic Polje, I used a megaphone to call on Muslims to surrender, that I killed a certain number of citizens of Muslim nationality, and did other things such as singling out Muslims fit for military service while they were being transported. I say that this gossip is untrue and that I did not do any of this, which can be confirmed by Mirko Jankovic who was with me all the time." Mr. Nikolic, do you still stand by your statement that you gave here with regard to this incident?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me -- what you read to us is that that witness read something in a newspaper about what Mr. Nikolic would have said. So it is -- now my question, your follow-up question is -- I have difficulties in relating that to what you just read to us. Could you clarify? Because if you read something in the newspaper that Mr. A says B, there are two matters to be verified: First, whether Mr. A said something, said B; and the second is whether B is true or not. These are two separate questions. Could you please keep that in mind and put the question in such a way that the Judges also understand what the link is to what you just read. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, just to make sure I can see where the Defence is going. They just read out a statement from the Blagojevic trial. I don't have the witness's name in front of me. And the assertion was: This witness says you were not in Konjevic Polje and asserts that he did not see you in Konjevic Polje. They have now moved onto the statement, which apparently they are putting in for the truth, from Mirko Jankovic, which we've just discussed, and this statement, the English we have, says Mirko Jankovic says he was in Konjevic Polje at that time with Momir Nikolic and that Momir Nikolic got out of the APC in Konjevic Polje. So what is their case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, any answer to that? If we are talking about this statement. First of all, we haven't read the whole of the statement so we have difficulties to see the context of it. I just focused on the small portion you read about rumours in newspapers and what everyone read in the newspapers. Could you please tackle the subject in an organised way, and first of all make clear to the Chamber, and perhaps to the witness, what your case is as far as the presence of Mr. Nikolic in -- in that location is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the part where I quoted Mr. Nikolic's statement, I wanted to ask him what his comment is on Petrovic's position; i.e., that he did not commit those murders.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by your leave, I can be of assistance. I know what Mr. Petrusic is aiming for. I am aware of this statement. I read it. I am even aware of the witness's evidence in one of the cases including mine. He appeared here before this Tribunal before I was sentenced. Mile Petrovic in his evidence before this Tribunal did not deny the fact that he was on the road between Bratunac and Konjevic Polje. He did not deny the fact that he was in the APC. He was in two minds whether to admit that he used a megaphone to invite people but there are video-clips showing that clearly. There is a video-clip clearly showing that he was calling out from the white APC on the Sandici-Konjevic Polje road. One thing that Mile Petrovic did not admit - and I really never expected him that he would - he didn't admit that, in Konjevic Polje, once I told him to take away two imprisoned Muslims and to link them up with a group that was already there. He denied here that he had killed them. He denied that he had done that. I did not expect him to admit. However, he admitted everything else. He admitted to the truth of everything else. He admitted that we received six Muslims on that road. All those elements that I spoke about, he confirmed them all but the last one; i.e., he never said that it was true that he had killed them. This is what I know from both his evidence and his statement. I hope I have been of some assistance in that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, is it the position of the Defence that Mr. Nikolic was not at that point in time in Konjevic Polje or is it the position of the Defence that Mr. Nikolic was in Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The position of the Defence is that on the 13th of July, Mr. Nikolic was in the -- on the cross-roads at Konjevic Polje but that did he not meet with General Mladic that afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you earlier asked the witness whether he refuted a statement saying that, "I didn't see Mr. Nikolic in Konjevic Polje." What's the use of that if it is your position that he was in Konjevic Polje? It's a waste of time. It's inconsistent. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 65 ter 14717.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, this is an order for active combat dated 2nd of July, 1995. It was issued by the command of Drina Corps. On the last page we will see that it was signed by Major-General Milenko Zivanovic. Mr. Nikolic, did you and when did you have an opportunity to see this document before the beginning of the attack on Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the commander of the Bratunac Brigade showed this document to the command sometime one or perhaps two days before the attack was launched. Let me just see the date. The 2nd of July. It was at the earliest sometime between the 4th and the 5th of July the Commander Blagojevic showed us this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The entire command was present or at least its bigger part?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the command was present. I am not sure that the battalion commanders were also there. On that same day, there was another meeting which was also attended by the battalion commanders, so I can't be sure of that meeting but I know that the command was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On page 4 in the Serbian version and on page 5 in the English version, you will see a paragraph which is relative to the intelligence security, and you will find it -- intelligence support, you will find it under bullet point 10. If we move on to the following page in the Serbian version, you will see that it says in the third line that: The security organs and the military police will identify the collection sector for prisoners of war, the collection and providing security for the prisoners of war and war booty. In treating the prisoners of war and the population, fully adhere to the Geneva Conventions. Do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did the security and intelligence organ of the Bratunac Brigade have to work out in its order that part that refers to the intelligence support?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question doesn't make much sense in terms of its contents. I want to help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Don't help me.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to help you because I want to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A security organ does not issue orders. That's for one. A security organ doesn't issue any orders on any of the issues, and if you are asking me whether I as a security organ contributed and helped the commander to draft his order on the use of the forces of the Bratunac Brigade, then we are talking about a different thing and I will answer. But security organs never, ever issue any orders. They don't write any orders. They don't submit any orders to anybody on any of the issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, I did not ask you whether you were the one who drafted orders. I asked you whether you participated in the drafting of bullet point 10, which refers to the intelligence support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we now have one clear question: Did you participate in the drafting of bullet point 10? That's the question. Of the document which is on your screen. Did you or did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I jump in for a moment and put a question to the witness. Mr. Petrusic read a part of this bullet point 10 to you, referring to the Geneva Conventions, and you confirmed that you found that sentence. Is this sentence in the B/C/S version in handwriting or is it typed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "In all dealings with prisoners of war and the civilian population abide by the Geneva Conventions." This is typed up. This is typed up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I put this question because in the English version we see that there is one sentence which is crossed out and behind that handwritten I read: "The sector for collecting war prisoners and war booty is the Pribicevac sector. In all dealings with prisoners of war and the civilian population abide by the Geneva Conventions." The second part of this is not in handwriting where the Geneva Conventions is referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there is a handwritten sentence in superscript. I'm going to read it: [As read] "The sector for collecting prisoners of war and war booty is the Pribicevac sector."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's all in handwriting, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, what I have just read out to you. That's in handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is not clear from the English translation. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, I'm looking at the clock. It is time for a break. Could we first have the witness escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, will you finish in the next session?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very quickly after the beginning of the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we take a break and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, we are still on the order issued by the Drina Corps on the 2nd of July. When you're looking at the B/C/S version and when you're looking at the part that was added by hand, where it says that the Pribicevac sector is where prisoners of war and war booty would be collected, is this your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, this handwriting looks like mine but I was not the one who wrote this. I did not make any corrections to this order. However, it does look like the way I write.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So we will agree that this bullet point is relative to your organ, the security and intelligence organ?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know who else may have been involved in that topic in the command of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Besides the commander, I don't think that there would have been anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Does this handwriting look like Commander Blagojevic's handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't the first question whether the handwriting was put on this document before or after it was issued? Because what we see, if we look at the original, there is a version which is signed and which is stamped and there are various stamps on it. Therefore, my first question would be: Has this handwriting be added after or is it part of the drafting of this document? Do you have any knowledge about that? Because sometimes you would find at my desk a document which is an official document, nevertheless, with my notes and handwriting on it, which is then not part of that document but is part of my version of the document with my annotations on it. I wonder which of the two is this document is. If the witness could tell us. Do you know whether this handwriting is put on the document after it had been delivered, sent, signed, or whether it was done before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I wouldn't be able to give a precise answer to that question. From what I see before me, by visual inspection, that is, what was written in the original was typed up, and only based on that I can infer that what is here in handwriting - and that is the sector for collecting prisoners of war and war booty is the sector of Pribicevac - that was written subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The whole document is full of handwritten changes, annotations, it's not only this part. Last page, for example, even changes apparently times. So if you don't know, then perhaps it's better to just tell us that you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I focused just on the part that you asked me about and my answer is: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We do not even know, Mr. Petrusic, as far as matters stand now, on whether the handwritten comments, corrections, et cetera, whether they are from the same person or from different persons, and added at the same time or at different times. It is a -- still a puzzle, at least for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to dwell upon that topic with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, if you look at the first page in this document, you will see that it was sent to the Zvornik, Bratunac, and the 2nd Romanija Brigades, to the Birac Brigade, to the 1st Milici Brigade, and to the 5th MAP. You will agree with me that if this part was added by hand before the document was dispatched to the units that I have just read out to you, then this handwritten bit should appear on all those documents, right? Am I right in thinking that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer in the affirmative but I wouldn't like to speculate. I told you what I knew about that part that was corrected. I don't know who made the corrections. I don't know when that was done on that page. I saw two different handwritings of which I know nothing. This is my problem. I can speculate and I agree with you on the question that you have just put to me, but I can't be certain because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, won't you, that on the last page it is quite clear that that document was received by the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the stamp, I would say, yes, it was received by the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, do you know who Dragoslav Trisic was or is?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 65 ter 1D01007, e-court page 79. This is the transcript of Mr. Dragoslav Trisic's evidence in the Popovic case on the 20th of October, 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: To -- the question: [As read] "Q. Tell me, please, you identified this handwriting in the upper margin as the handwriting of Captain Momir Nikolic; is that the case? "A. Yes. "Q. You were personally there when he wrote this, right? "A. Well, I recognise his handwriting. "Q. Do you know when he wrote this? "A. Well, I suppose that he did it on the day when we received the aforementioned document." So let's stop there. That was from the transcript. What is your position with regard to the statement provided by Mr. Trisic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would object, Your Honour, because he's already answered question of whether it's his handwriting, and I -- based on the discussion we had earlier, I don't know if it's -- there is any point in him commenting on what or why Mr. Trisic testified this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness said it's not his handwriting although it has similarity. That is what the witness told us. If you have any further questions to the witness, please put them to him, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which document?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter -- I apologise, 65 ter 14717, which is the Drina Corps order that we discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We saw 1D1006. Okay. Thank you. It was my mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection to 14717, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And again I have not written it down. Is that the Drina Corps order, the six pages with the handwriting on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 14717 receives number D302, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. One of the thoughts that came to my mind, not only looking at the handwritten portion but also at, for example, the -- striking through parts of the text which on the last page, which, by the way, doesn't appear clearly in the translation, that this may have been a document which was received and then was -- further work was done on it perhaps to convey the order to lower-level units. That's a thought that came into my mind and which I want to share with the parties because if they have any comments on it, then I'd like to hear from them. And it is especially that the change of times at the very end of the order could serve such a purpose. I leave it to that. But, of course, the Chamber has to understand what this document is about. Mr. Petrusic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at 65 ter 05803, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, you recognise the document. This is the order for active combat operations issued by the 1st Bratunac Infantry Brigade on the 5th of July, 1995. On the last page you will see that it's signed by Colonel Vidoje Blagojevic. First I would like to ask you if this order came about as the result of an order by the Drina Corps dated the 2nd of July?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And this order by the Bratunac Brigade command, was it drafted by all the command organs?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me who provides the commander with estimates of enemy strength?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Intelligence organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And that is you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And in this case, did Commander Blagojevic ask you for an estimate on the enemy strength?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we're going to move to page 10 -- actually, page 4 in the Serbian version, paragraph 10, and then in the English version it's page 5. Item 5 [as interpreted] begins with combat security and intelligence security. Can we look at page 5 of the B/C/S version, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's not item 5 but item 10 on page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Item 10 on page 5, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Item 10 on page 5, not the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. Perhaps it's a matter of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, this item 10, intelligence security, who proposes that to the commander?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The intelligence security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And in this specific case that was done by you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should have been me but I did not do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And can you please tell me who did?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the Court permits me, I would just like to clarify absolutely because I can see that we are struggling with both of the orders, so I would like to ask for three minutes to explain exactly what happened and then everything will be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could try to do it in one minute, that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best. When an order is written or a commander's decision, regardless of whether it's at the corps or brigade level -- anyway I'm going to speak now about the Bratunac Brigade --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, for interrupting the witness, and you did give him the time, but I do apologise. I would just like to ask you to stop the witness in as far as his testimony could focus on some kind of expert evidence. What I would like to limit him to is just to say "yes" or "no" and say whether he took part in the drafting of this item or not, and if he did not, then he could say who drafted the -- that part, that item.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is precisely what I am going to talk about. This is precisely what I am going to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please do so. I had not the feeling that any expert evidence was coming up, but could you tell us who, then, drafted this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The complete - the complete - order for the use of the units of the Bratunac Brigade was written by the commander of my brigade, Colonel Blagojevic. This order is -- there are two ways to write an order. There are two ways to actually draft an order of this kind. The first way is the regular procedure when the brigade commander, together with his assistants, sits in the office and on the basis of the Drina Corps commander's order prepares his own order for the engagement of his own units. And then in this regular procedure, this is done when you have enough time at your disposal, then each assistant commander, as part of the commander's order that he would sign, gives his contribution. I as the intelligence organ would make my contribution. That would be the first item of the order, that would be the data about the enemy. And then as part of that same order, I would also give two other things to the commander and that would be the proposal by -- for intelligence security protection or support and then the proposal for security support. I propose that to the commander and I also take part in the writing of the order for the use of reconnaissance units. These are things that are done in the regular procedure. Since we received the order on the 2nd of July, and we were supposed to be ready for attack on the 6th of July at 4.00 a.m., then my commander - this is very important - my commander participated the entire time in the preparation of the order of the Drina Corps command. He went there and he took part in the preparation of the Drina Corps order so that my commander had all of these things that had to do with the -- my part of the job, that would be paragraph 1, data about the enemy, and intelligence and security support, which was also supposed to have had come from me. So he returned to Bratunac and then my commander used his discretionary powers, and on the basis of teamwork in which he participated at the Drina Corps level, he used his discretionary right and wrote, on the basis of the Drina Corps order, his order. He just extracted the tasks entrusted to the Bratunac Brigade and he wrote his order for the Bratunac Brigade. So that would be a truncated procedure. It does not imply all of the above. He can consult his assistants in the truncated procedure, but if he has sufficient information about all the combat-readiness elements, then he can write the order himself. In both cases - this is a very important sentence - in both cases, the brigade commander -- you can suggest whatever you want at this joint meeting, the brigade commander can accept your proposal or suggestion, he can accept a part of it, or he can reject your entire proposal and say, "I have decided ..." When the commander says, "I have decided ...," then everything that you've said before is done with. The commander makes his decision. There are no more proposals and suggestions. So I have tried my best to clarify this whole matter. I hope that it was worth it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You are trying to say that he wrote the entire order, Blagojevic, based on the information that he had at his disposal?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am saying that that was the result of his decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, do you see that this order that we can see on our screens states that the sector of Pribicevac was assigned as the sector where the prisoners should gather and that is added by hand in the Drina Corps order?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And was this done by Colonel Blagojevic in the Bratunac Brigade order?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that is in this order is something that was his responsibility. He was the commander. He's the only person authorised to sign the order and he did sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now go back to the last page of this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And we will see that the Pribicevac IKM of the brigade became functional or operational from 1200 hours. Do you need to look at the previous order by the Drina Corps on the screen which states that the IKM - it was crossed out - of the brigade was in the Pribicevac sector. And then 1600 hours was crossed out, and then 1200 hours was written by hand. Do you need to look at that order on your screen to compare the two?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is no need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So did Commander Blagojevic, as you say, make these changes and include them entirely in his order based on the changes made in the Drina Corps order?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not make that kind of comparison, but what I see is more or less defined also in the Drina Corps order only with different times. I think the time there is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender 65 ter 05803.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of any objections, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 05803 receives number D303, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, from the -- the attack on Srebrenica started on the 6th of July and the forward command post of the Bratunac Brigade was located at Pribicevac from that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Were you at Pribicevac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the 6th, yes. After the 6th, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And from the 6th to the 11th?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not at Pribicevac then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us, as briefly as possible, whether you were stationed at the Bratunac Brigade command during that period?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not for the Bratunac Brigade command. I was dealing or responsible for the area of responsibility of my unit, including the check-point at Zuti Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you have information about when General Mladic would arrive at the Bratunac Brigade area of responsibility during the combat operations?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you precisely when I got information the first time that he would arrive, but I know approximately when they announced that General Mladic would come. I can tell by the combat. Combat was being carried out along that axis. At the beginning there was some kind of success by Serbian forces, and then perhaps on the second or third day, but I cannot be sure about that, problems cropped up. I even think that on that day, one or two Serbian soldiers were killed, one was seriously wounded, and the operation halted. I don't know. I don't know what was happening between General Krstic and the corps command along that line, but I know that General Mladic arrived around that time when the operation ground to a halt.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And do you know that at that time there was a major storm in Bratunac, Srebrenica, and the surrounding area, and that that was the reason for halting the operation on the 7th and the 8th of July, 1995? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And who informed you that General Mladic would come at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know exactly, but I did have information that he was supposed to arrive. I don't remember who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And did you go then to secure the road from Konjevic Polje to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And did you secure the Bratunac-Pribicevac road which was taken by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Tell me, you did it again with a military police platoon?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that members of the military police were involved, and I also think that elements of a reconnaissance platoon were also involved, but I believe that the majority of them were military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you meet General Mladic at Bratunac at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to General Mladic in the course of those days?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Your first conversation with him, according to you, took place in Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My first encounter with General Mladic in that period was at Hotel Fontana on the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that the two of you talked on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I want to say is that I met General Mladic when he arrived at Hotel Fontana to attend the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you report to him on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. It was Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: My question was: Did you talk to General Mladic on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We greeted each other, General Mladic arrived, three of us met him, and we exchanged some phrases that were an expression of good manners but were irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When the war started in 1992 up until July 1995, how many times did you have an opportunity to talk to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it happened on two occasions: Once when I was summoned to Crna Rijeka, and I believe that it had to do with talks about the enclave boundaries, and I brought a report on that issue with me that had been requested from me to provide. And the next time, I think it was in 1994, when General Mladic visited my brigade and I was in his escort when he visited the 2nd Infantry Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, the simple question was: How many times. The answer, the simple answer is: Two times. If Mr. Petrusic wants to know more, then he'll ask you about it. Mr. Petrusic, because the subject matter may be totally irrelevant. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, in the agreement on facts and acceptance of responsibility, paragraph 9, you said: "I spent about 45 minutes in Konjevic Polje prior to the arrival of General Mladic. He arrived there by car from the direction of Bratunac and he stopped at an intersection at Konjevic Polje. He alighted from the vehicle, and we met in the middle of the road. I reported to him and said that there were no problems. He looked around him and he saw prisoners. Some of those prisoners asked him what was going to happen to them, to which he responded that all of them would be taken away from there and that they shouldn't worry." This is what you stated on the 6th of May, 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, I see that the staff is very active in getting paragraph 9 on the screen, but since you have not given any source they are still with the previous document. So if you could give a number so that we can follow what you are reading and not look at paragraph 9 of the former document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I apologise, Your Honours, but speaking about the previous document, which is still on our screens, which is 65 ter 14717, I would like to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have admitted it already, Mr. Petrusic. I think the two of them, the original Drina Corps order and this one, Bratunac Brigade, were already admitted. But if you would focus on what I asked you, that is to give the number of the document you are reading from, then we could move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's document D301. And that's paragraph 9, the passage last but one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Nikolic, there is no need for me to read this paragraph again. You can see it on your screen. And here you described your encounter with General Mladic in the agreement. Although, yet again, you never mentioned in this agreement that General Mladic, in response to your question what would happen with them, made a certain movement with his hand.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: After this agreement was concluded, you spent another four days or had another four interviews with the Prosecution. That was on the 28th, 29th, and 30th May, and 12th of July. Do you remember these conversations?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that there were a lot of interviews. I cannot remember every single one of them. But I did talk to the Prosecution several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And in these conversations, you never mentioned a certain gesture that Mr. Mladic made with his hand with respect to what would happen to those people.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I demonstrated that or not, but if it's not recorded, then I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: But do you remember, to the best of your recollection, when did you first say or made such a gesture that General Mladic allegedly made in Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Maybe in one of my testimonies, but I don't know precisely when.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you cite at least one reason why you failed to do that before?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Probably nobody asked me about it. When I gave evidence, I did my best to provide every possible detail about what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Well, wouldn't you say that this alleged gesture with his hand should have featured in all these interviews? Don't you think that you should have mentioned it in every conversation that you had with regard to the facts and responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that is contained in the agreement was authored by my defence counsel, and that was not the only oversight and lapse on their part, and I ascribe responsibility to my lawyers. And it's a great responsibility. They, themselves, admitted that they failed to do that, and in their mutual correspondence they conceded to the fact that this part that should have been formulated in a proper legal manner was not done as it should have been done due to the fact -- and that was one of the reasons why this is not contained here and why in my subsequent statements I had to provide an accurate description of what I said. There is no other explanation than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Nikolic, I can agree with you that in your subsequent statements you provided a lot of information that you disagreed with. And you did that on the 27th of April, 2007, and to the best of my recollection, all of that was accepted. In this supplementary statement, you said that your encounter with General Mladic happened in the way you described and that that was the moment when General Mladic made the gesture in question.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not one of the corrections that I made because I believed that it was not of any significance and that was probably the reason why I never mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I suppose you will agree with me that this alleged gesture made by General Mladic took place at Konjevic Polje, and it was a very interesting, not to say key, moment both for the Prosecution and all other concerned parties. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that to be a crucial piece of information or anything else that would be valuable for the Prosecution. There are many more other things in the gestures of your client that there -- this is actually a minor thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, did you have an opportunity to see this statement during the break? The statement that was put to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you give it to the Registrar to be given to Mr. Nikolic and then -- so that he could read it? No. Then if no one cares about giving it to him, then he'll not receive it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I never received any statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since I would not disallow that you give it for the next break and then ask one or two questions after the break, but preferably it should have been done already. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, which vehicle did General Mladic use to get to Pribicevac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly because I didn't see him personally leave for Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions for Mr. Nikolic and with this I would like to conclude my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrusic. I suggest that we take a break a little bit earlier, that you provide -- Mr. Petrusic, that the Defence provides the witness with the document that you had in mind, that is the statement of another witness, as far as I understand. Could you also clearly indicate what portions you would expect the witness to read, and then after the break, you'll have another five minutes to put some questions on that. And after that, Mr. Nicholls, you'll have an opportunity to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just -- I have a hard copy in the Serbian language if it -- if they need one, of this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Petrusic, that you'll gladly accept this assistance. Then could the usher give it -- but you can't indicate which portions the witness should read --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I suggest, Mr. Petrusic, do you have a hard copy of the document in your own language? The document you wish the witness to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there any comments on it or is it a virgin document?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document is not exactly clear, but the only comment is an indication which one of those is an English version and which one is the Serbian version, but I should have made a copy before anything was added by hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, do you have a clean copy in the Serbian or the B/C/S language?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I do have a clean copy if --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, if -- then --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry. I do have a clean copy that has nothing on. I don't know if my friend wants to see it first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the clean copy -- how long is the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Three pages, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Three pages. Then I think it's a waste of time to indicate what the witness should read. Mr. Nikolic, you are invited to read all three pages during the break. And could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom together with the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break and we will resume at five minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, can you tell us, how far was General Mladic's escort at the time when you purportedly reported to him at Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- well, you know just as I do, what is the distance between an officer and his escort, five steps, ten steps, up to 15. That's standard procedure. There is nothing special about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did they ever get out of the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And you were a few steps in front of them as well as General Mladic? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first walked towards General Mladic, and once I finished my reporting to him, then we walked together some 20 paces towards the people who were prisoners there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that that was the only police check-point at this intersection in Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was another one in Kravica. But in Konjevic Polje, yes, there was only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: At this police check-point or, rather, in that area, there were no visible obstacles that would separate you and General Mladic from the remaining personnel in the area?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The Defence position is -- because, sir, you also said that General Mladic addressed the prisoners. Therefore, the Defence position, Mr. Nikolic, is that at this location, at this point, there were no visual -- visually noticeable imprisoned Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to quote a part of the statement, 65 ter 1D01002. That is Mladen Blagojevic's statement, who says on page 2, paragraph 4 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First, is it clear, Mr. Petrusic, that you put this to the witness as a follow-up - because you were given an opportunity to discuss the documents with the witness - is this a follow-up on where the witness said where Mr. Mladic addressed the prisoners or the men detained, and now you are reading a portion of a statement which says otherwise. Is that what we are at? Then please have it on the screen so that we can follow the reading and see something of the context and then read -- oh, it's already. I apologise. It's already on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's English page 2, paragraph 3, the last sentence, which reads --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And Blagojevic says: "At the intersection, there were no persons for who I could have concluded that they were captured Muslims." Mr. Nikolic, can you tell us, did Mr. Blagojevic have any reason at all to claim otherwise or contrary to what you said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Form of the question. I don't know that the witness can tell us what was in Mr. Blagojevic's mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that Mr. Petrusic wanted to ask whether there is any fact known to this witness which might lead him -- which might be relevant for understanding why Mr. Blagojevic gave a different -- statement different from his account of the event. That is what Mr. Petrusic apparently wanted to ask you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? Yes. I cannot answer this question without mentioning one absurd statement from the statement -- or, rather, something that is absolutely untrue. In his statement, Mr. Blagojevic said that he saw around 100 imprisoned Muslim in -- in Sandici, and he also said that in Sandici, General Mladic got out of the vehicle and addressed the Muslims. Then he arrived in Konjevic Polje where, on the 13th, there was the largest number of Muslims who were taken prisoner. So to be precise, from Kamenica, Konjevic Polje, almost to the Kuslat sector. So this is a pretty large area and the assertion that Blagojevic, who were there, did not see any prisoner is -- is untrue because they were there. It was impossible not to see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you are contesting the accuracy of the statement. We leave it to that. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, those military policemen, were they in a position to see everything that you and General Mladic gesticulated? Could they hear and see or one of the two? What was going on during your encounter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Focused question, please, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: This refers to -- or, rather, in terms of where they were vis-a-vis you and General Mladic, could military policemen see that alleged gesture with his hand that General Mladic made?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could see everything I did. They could see my encounter with General Mladic. They could both see and hear my report, because I did it quite loudly. Whether they did see on and hear everything, I don't know. I don't know what they heard or saw. Whether they were focused, whether they were paying enough attention, I wouldn't be able to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 5 on page 2, in English it's the fourth paragraph, this same witness says, and I quote: "I can also state that on that occasion, on the 13th of July, at the intersection, I did not see Momir Nikolic talking to General Mladic at the police check-point." Further on: "If Momir Nikolic is claiming to have met and spoken with General Mladic at that location at the intersection in Konjevic Polje on that day and that General Mladic then indicated to him with a motion of the arm that the Muslims would be liquidated, I state categorically that this is not true." This is to be found in paragraph 5 of this statement. Mr. Nikolic, what is your position vis-a-vis this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My position vis-a-vis the entire statement is special. There are parts - including this paragraph - which are absolutely incorrect, and particularly this paragraph is incorrect. If I have to go through the statement and tell you what is not correct, I am prepared to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: No, that won't be necessary. I am here to put questions to you. Will you allow for a possibility that while you were in Konjevic Polje, you popped in to some of the nearby houses along the road?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When you went to fetch Resid Sinanovic, did you enter the house where he was?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Resid Sinanovic was brought by the members of the police to my car, as far as I can remember. That was 18 years ago, and I'm speaking from memory. However, I knew that there was some other detained Muslims in the same house where Resid Sinanovic was. They were young and it was obvious they were members of the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to tender this document into evidence, and that would be all I had for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, I have no further questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, am I supposed to return the statement to somebody?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The usher will take it back from you. Mr. Petrusic, are you tendering this document for the -- for the truth of its content, and then not whether Mr. Blagojevic said it but whether what he said is to be relied upon? Is that the purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bearing in mind that the primary reason for the admission is the truthfulness of the statement which the Defence deems to be true, this is the reason for admission. However, bearing in mind that it's -- that the relevant parts of the transcript of the statement have been quoted, in this case we can withdraw our motion for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because there might be a problem. The statement is drawn -- was drafted for the purposes of this Tribunal, and then Rule 92 bis, 92 ter, 92 quater would apply as a lex specialis to the general rules on evidence. But it being withdrawn, we don't need to pay further attention to it. Thank you, Mr. Petrusic. These were your questions. Mr. Nicholls, any questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, just a few, Your Honours. I think my -- a couple more questions came up at the end, but I think I will still be less than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, let me go back -- let's talk about Konjevic Polje and the gesture. I have to switch mics. At page 36 of the transcript today, Mr. Petrusic quoted from paragraph 9 of your statement of facts about your encounter with General Mladic at Konjevic Polje.
